Pre-fetch rates for every currency pair at the start of each run and attach all of them to every prompt
why: A scoped cross-role tool removes round trips for the frequent, simple need while the rare complex case still flows through the coordinator. Handing over the whole finance toolset breaks specialization, memory-based rates are unreliable, and pre-fetching everything bloats every prompt.

q: A research subagent has a fetch_url tool that can retrieve any address, and it sometimes fetches login pages, ads and search-result pages instead of source documents. Which change is best?
opts: Add a prompt line telling it to avoid login pages, ads and search-result pages when fetching
Give it a second, slower fetch tool that it can fall back on when the first returns junk
Increase the tool timeout so that pages finish loading completely before they are read
Replace fetch_url with a load_document tool that validates the address and returns text
why: Replacing a broad generic tool with a constrained one builds the guardrail into the interface. A prompt request is probabilistic, a backup fetcher shares the same flaw, and a longer timeout does nothing about fetching the wrong kind of page.

q: An intake service defines one extraction tool per document type (invoice, receipt, contract), and the type of an incoming file is unknown. Sometimes the model replies "This looks like an invoice" in plain text and calls nothing. Which setting guarantees a structured tool call?
opts: tool_choice set to any, so some tool must be called and the model picks the matching one
tool_choice set to auto, which leaves the model free to decide whether to call anything at all
tool_choice forced to the invoice extraction tool, since invoices are the most common type
tool_choice set to none, with instructions asking for JSON in the text of the reply
why: Requiring some tool call while leaving the choice to the model fits an unknown document type. Automatic choice allows plain text, forcing the invoice tool is wrong for other types, and disabling tools removes structure altogether. If your model does not accept the require-any mode, use automatic choice with strict tool use and check that a tool call came back.

q: A document pipeline must always run extract_metadata first and then let the model choose among enrichment tools based on that metadata. Which approach is best?
opts: Set tool_choice to any on every request so that the model always has to call some tool
Force extract_metadata on the first request, then continue in later turns with automatic choice
Add "always call extract_metadata first" to the system prompt and keep automatic choice throughout
Force extract_metadata on every request, including the enrichment steps
why: Forcing the named tool for the first call guarantees that step happens first, and later turns return to automatic choice so the model can pick enrichment tools from the result. Requiring any tool does not fix the order, a prompt instruction is probabilistic, and forcing it every time would block the enrichment steps. On models that reject forced tool choice, run extract_metadata in application code first, or use automatic choice and check that the call came back.

q: A developer forces a specific tool and notices that the model never writes an explanation before the call, even when the prompt asks for one. Why, and what is the alternative?
opts: Forcing prefills the reply, so the call comes first; use automatic choice and ask for an explanation in the prompt
Strict tool use suppresses text blocks in the reply, so disable strict mode and send the request again
The temperature is too low for chatty replies, so raise it until the model adds some commentary first
Forced calls ignore system prompts entirely, so move the instruction into the tool description instead
why: When a tool is required or forced, the API prefills the reply so the model emits the tool call directly, without a natural-language preamble. For explanation plus a call, leave tool choice on automatic and instruct the model in the prompt. Strict mode, temperature and prompt placement are not the cause.

q: Which pairing of goal and tool_choice setting is correct?
opts: Model decides: any. Must call a specific tool: auto. Must call some tool, any one: the named form of the setting
Model decides: the named form. Must call some tool: auto. Must call a specific tool: none
Model decides: auto. Must call some tool, any one: any. Must call a specific tool: the named form
Model decides: none. Must call some tool: auto. Must call a specific tool: any
why: Automatic choice leaves the decision to the model, "any" guarantees a call but lets the model pick which tool, and the named form guarantees one particular tool. The other pairings scramble these meanings.

q: In a research system with search, analysis and report specialists, which tool set is most appropriate for the coordinator?
opts: Every tool of every specialist, so that it can step in directly whenever one of them fails
The web-search and document-parsing tools, because it needs to verify the specialists' work
No tools at all, since all it does is write prompts and read the replies it gets back
The subagent-launching tool plus light coordination utilities, not the specialists' working tools
why: The coordinator delegates; it should hold the means to spawn subagents and little else, so that its decisions stay about orchestration. Giving it every specialist tool recreates the overload problem, and with no tools at all it could not delegate.

q: A team wants every developer who clones the repository to have the same Jira MCP server available, and nobody should paste tokens into chat or commit them. What is the best setup?
opts: Each developer adds the server to their own user config and pastes the shared token into that file
Commit .mcp.json with the token written in plain text, since the repository is private and access-controlled
Commit .mcp.json with the server and a ${JIRA_TOKEN} reference; each developer sets the variable locally
Describe the server in CLAUDE.md and ask each developer to configure it by hand following the notes
why: The project-scoped .mcp.json travels with version control, and environment variable expansion keeps credentials out of it. Personal configs defeat sharing, a plain-text token in a repository is a leak waiting to happen, and CLAUDE.md is guidance for the model, not server configuration.

q: A developer wants to try an experimental MCP server across all of her projects without affecting teammates. Where should it be configured?
opts: At user scope, in her own ~/.claude.json
In the project's committed .mcp.json
In the repository's CLAUDE.md
In every teammate's settings, so everyone can compare results
why: User-scoped servers are private to the person and available in all her projects, which fits personal or experimental tooling. The committed project file and teammates' settings would impose the experiment on others, and CLAUDE.md does not configure servers.

q: A project-scoped GitHub server is committed in .mcp.json, and a developer also adds a personal experimental server at user scope. Which tools can the agent use during a session?
opts: Only the project server's tools, since the shared scope always overrides the personal one
Only the personal server's tools, because the user scope has priority over the project scope
Tools from one server at a time, which the developer switches with a slash command in the session
Tools from both servers at once, since all configured servers' tools are available together
why: Tools from every configured server are discovered at connection and available simultaneously. Scope precedence only matters when the same server name is defined in more than one place, and then the whole higher-precedence entry wins.

q: An agent supporting a large documentation site spends many calls just discovering which pages exist before it reads any. Which MCP capability best reduces this overhead?
opts: A search tool with extra optional filters for section, date and page type
A resource that exposes the documentation hierarchy as a catalog the agent sees up front
A larger model with a bigger context window to hold more search results
A prompt template that tells the agent to guess likely page names from the site map
why: Resources are designed to expose content such as documentation hierarchies, issue summaries or schemas, so the agent knows what exists without exploratory calls. More search filters still require searching, a bigger model does not remove the discovery calls, and guessing page names is unreliable.

q: A custom MCP server offers find_symbol_usages, which understands code symbols, but the agent keeps reaching for the built-in text search instead. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Disable the built-in text search for every project so that the agent has no other choice but to use the MCP tool
Add a system-prompt rule that says "never use text search" for any kind of question about code
Expand the MCP tool's description: what it does beyond text search, what it returns, when to prefer it
Rename the tool to plain "search" so that it sounds like the familiar built-in one
why: Agents choose tools from their descriptions, and a thin MCP description loses to a familiar built-in. Describing the capability and output in detail fixes the cause. Disabling the built-in is heavy-handed, a blanket prompt ban is brittle, and a vague name adds confusion.

q: A team needs access to Jira and also needs a workflow that applies its own release-calendar rules. What is the best plan?
opts: Use an existing Jira MCP server; build a small custom server only for the release-calendar rules
Build custom servers for both, to keep everything consistent and under the team's control
Use an existing Jira server and encode the release-calendar rules in a long system prompt
Build a custom Jira server, then look for a community server that handles release calendars
why: Adopt maintained community servers for standard integrations and reserve custom servers for team-specific workflows. Custom Jira code is unnecessary maintenance, and putting rules that need computation into a prompt is unreliable.

q: A teammate committed .mcp.json containing "Authorization": "Bearer ghp_abc123…" in plain text. How should the file be written, and what else is needed?
opts: Base64-encode the token in the file, which hides it from casual readers, with no further action
Add .mcp.json to .gitignore and share the file with teammates by email or chat instead
Move the token into CLAUDE.md, which servers never read, so the config file stays clean
Reference "Bearer ${GITHUB_TOKEN}", set it per environment, and rotate the exposed token
why: Environment variable expansion lets the committed file contain only a reference, with secrets supplied per machine. The leaked token must also be rotated. Encoding is not protection, ignoring the file defeats team sharing, and CLAUDE.md is not a secrets store.

q: You want to expose (a) a read-only listing of database schemas that the agent can use as context and (b) an action that creates an order. Which MCP primitives fit?
opts: Both should be tools, because tools can return any kind of data
(a) should be a resource and (b) should be a tool
(a) should be a prompt and (b) should be a resource
Both should be prompts, so that the user chooses when each is used
why: Resources carry content for context, here the schemas, while tools perform actions that may have side effects, here order creation. Prompts are user-selected templates, so they fit neither need.

q: You need every file in a large monorepo whose name ends in .test.tsx. Which built-in tool is the best fit?
opts: Grep, searching file contents for the string ".test.tsx"
Read, opening each directory in turn and looking for matching names
Glob, using a path pattern such as **/*.test.tsx
Edit, supplying a list of the paths that should match
why: Finding files by name or extension is path pattern matching, which is what Glob does. Grep searches inside file contents, Read loads a known file, and Edit modifies text.

q: To find every place that calls calculateTax across a codebase, which approach fits best?
opts: Search file contents for the function name with Grep
Use Glob with the pattern *tax* to find the files that mention it
Read every source file in order and note the callers as they appear
Write a new file that lists the callers from memory of the codebase
why: Locating callers is a search of file contents for a name, which is Grep's job. A name pattern only finds files called tax, reading everything is slow and context-heavy, and writing from memory invents data.

q: A configuration file contains six identical lines "timeout: 30". You need to change only the one inside the [payments] section. The targeted edit fails because the text matches more than once. What is the right next step?
opts: Repeat the same edit with replace-all enabled so that it definitely applies, accepting all six changes
Run a content search for the line and write the search output back as the new file contents
Delete the file and recreate it entirely from memory of what the configuration should contain
Add neighboring lines to make the anchor unique, or read the file and write the updated whole
why: A targeted edit needs a unique anchor. Adding distinguishing context makes one, and when that is impractical, reading the file and writing the full updated content is the reliable fallback. Replace-all would change all six lines, and the other options discard or invent content.

q: Asked to explain how refunds flow through an unfamiliar 3,000-file service, what is the best first step?
opts: Read every file in the repository first, in directory order, to build a complete picture before answering
Search for entry points such as refund routes, then read only the files needed to follow the imports
List all files with Glob and read the largest ones first, since they hold the most logic
Ask the user to name every file that is relevant before starting any search at all
why: Building understanding incrementally, from a targeted search for entry points to reading just the files the trail leads to, keeps context focused. Reading everything exhausts context, size says nothing about relevance, and asking the user delays work the agent can do itself.

q: The function formatPrice is re-exported as fmtPrice and money by two wrapper modules. Searching for "formatPrice" finds only its definition and two callers, but the team suspects more usages. What should the agent do?
opts: Search again for "formatPrice" with more surrounding context lines
Use Glob to list the wrapper modules and assume every file that imports them is a caller
List the names each wrapper exports, then search the codebase for each of those names
Read the test files and infer the usages from the test names
why: Callers that use a wrapper's alias never contain the original name, so the agent must first find the exported names and then search for each. More context lines cannot find a different identifier, and assuming every importer is a caller overcounts.

q: Which situation best justifies reading a file and rewriting it with Write instead of making a targeted edit?
opts: The text identifying the change location occurs several times and cannot be made unique
A one-line fix whose surrounding text is unique and easy to quote exactly in the edit request
Renaming a function whose name appears only once in a very large file with many other definitions
Inserting a one-line comment above a line that is unique in the file and easy to anchor on
why: Write replaces the whole file, so it is the fallback when no unique anchor exists for a targeted edit. In the other cases a unique anchor is available, and a small edit is cheaper and less risky than rewriting a file.

q: You must find which Markdown files under docs/ mention the phrase "rate limit". Which approach is most efficient?
opts: Read every file under docs/ one by one and scan each of them for the phrase
Use Glob with the pattern "rate limit" to find the files that contain that text
Use Edit to open each Markdown file under docs/ and look for the phrase
Use Grep for the phrase, restricted to Markdown files under docs/
why: This is a content search scoped to a file type and folder, which Grep supports directly. Glob matches names, not text, Edit modifies files, and reading everything is wasteful.

q: Which two elements make a tool description more effective? (Choose two.)
opts: Accepted input formats with an example
A boundary stating when to use a similar tool instead
Marketing language about how fast and reliable the tool is
Details of the tool's internal implementation
A single sentence that repeats the tool's name
why: Descriptions help the model choose and call a tool when they explain inputs, outputs, edge cases and the boundary against neighbors. Praise, implementation internals and repeating the name give no selection signal.

q: Which two actions fix misrouting between two tools with overlapping descriptions? (Choose two.)
opts: Rename each tool to reflect its distinct purpose
Rewrite the descriptions with inputs, outputs and boundaries
Add the same extra sentence to both descriptions
Set the sampling temperature to zero
Alphabetize the tool list
why: Overlap is a definition problem, so the fix is to give each tool a distinct name and a description that says what it is for and not for. Identical additions, temperature and ordering do not separate the tools.

q: Which two pieces of information help an agent choose a recovery after a tool fails? (Choose two.)
opts: An error category such as transient, validation, permission or business
Whether the call is worth retrying
The complete server stack trace
The name of the engineer who wrote the tool
A numeric internal code with no explanation
why: The category and the retryable flag, with a readable message, map directly onto recovery choices. Stack traces, authorship and bare codes are noise for the model.

q: A search subagent cannot resolve a timeout locally. Which two items should it send to the coordinator? (Choose two.)
opts: What it attempted, including the query and the failure type
Any partial results it gathered before the failure
A generic message saying search is unavailable
An empty result marked as successful
Only the raw exception object, with no explanation
why: Structured context about what was attempted and what was obtained lets the coordinator decide whether to retry differently, use another source, or continue with partial data. Generic statuses hide the details, and an empty success silently suppresses the error.

q: Which two statements about tool_choice are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: With automatic choice the model may answer in plain text instead of calling a tool
Requiring any tool guarantees a call but lets the model decide which tool
A forced named tool lets the model choose a different tool if it prefers
Setting it to none forces a call to the first tool in the list
Forcing a tool guarantees its arguments are semantically correct
why: Automatic choice leaves text responses possible, and "any" guarantees a call without naming the tool. Forcing a named tool leaves no choice, "none" disables tools, and no tool_choice setting can guarantee that the values themselves are right.

q: Which two changes improve tool selection reliability in a multi-agent system? (Choose two.)
opts: Give each subagent only the tools its role needs
Replace a generic fetch-any-URL tool with a validated document loader
Give every agent every tool so that none is ever blocked
Remove tool descriptions to save tokens
Rely on the prompt to tell each agent which tools to ignore
why: Smaller, role-specific toolsets and constrained tools reduce decision complexity and misuse. Giving everything to everyone, deleting descriptions and prompt-only restrictions all make selection worse or leave it to chance.

q: Which two statements about MCP configuration scopes are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: A committed .mcp.json shares its servers with everyone who uses the repository
User-scoped servers live in the user's own ~/.claude.json and are not shared
Project-scoped servers cannot use environment variables
Only one MCP server can be active at a time
User-scoped servers are committed to version control automatically
why: The project file is the shared one and the user-level file is private. Project files can use ${VAR} expansion, many servers can be active together, and nothing in the user config is committed automatically.

q: Which two are good reasons to expose data as an MCP resource rather than as a tool? (Choose two.)
opts: It is read-only content such as a documentation hierarchy or schema listing
It lets the agent see what exists without exploratory tool calls
It has to perform an action with side effects
It should be chosen by the user as a slash command
It must be invoked by the model only after approval
why: Resources suit read-only context and can serve as catalogs that cut exploratory calls. Actions with side effects are tools, and user-selected templates are prompts.

q: Which two tasks are best handled by a content search such as Grep? (Choose two.)
opts: Finding every call to a particular function
Locating where a specific error message is raised
Listing all files that have a given extension
Replacing the text of one unique line
Creating a new configuration file
why: Content search finds lines inside files, such as callers and error strings. Listing by extension is Glob, replacing text is Edit, and creating files is Write.

q: Which two statements about built-in file tools are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: Edit replaces exact existing text, which must match and be unique in the file
Write replaces the whole file with the content supplied
Glob searches the inside of files for matching lines
Read modifies files in place
Grep lists files by their extension only
why: Edit is a targeted exact-match replacement and Write supplies a complete file. Glob matches paths rather than contents, Read only loads files, and content search looks at what is inside files.

q: Tool descriptions are the main information the model uses to decide which tool to call.
opts: True
False
why: The model chooses from the descriptions and schemas it is shown, which is why thin descriptions lead to unreliable selection.

q: Two tools with near-identical descriptions are likely to be confused with each other even if their names differ.
opts: True
False
why: Overlapping descriptions leave the model without a basis for choosing, so calls get misrouted. Distinct purposes and boundaries are needed.

q: System-prompt wording can accidentally bias the model toward a particular tool even when the tool descriptions are accurate.
opts: True
False
why: Keyword-heavy instructions can create unintended associations between a topic and a tool, overriding what the descriptions say.

q: A tool error that only says "Operation failed" gives the agent enough information to choose between retrying and escalating.
opts: True
False
why: A uniform message hides whether the failure is transient, a validation problem, a policy refusal or a permission issue, so the agent cannot choose a sensible recovery.

q: A business-rule violation, such as a refund requested outside the allowed window, should be reported as not retryable.
opts: True
False
why: Repeating the call cannot change a policy outcome. Flag it as final and include wording the agent can pass to the customer.

q: A query that ran successfully and returned zero matches should be reported as a failure so the agent retries it.
opts: True
False
why: No matches is a valid result. Reporting it as a failure would trigger pointless retries and blur the difference from a real access failure.

q: Setting tool_choice to auto guarantees that the model calls at least one tool.
opts: True
False
why: Automatic choice lets the model answer in plain text. Requiring some tool, or forcing a named one, is what guarantees a call.

q: Forcing a specific tool is one way to make sure that a particular step runs before the model decides what to do next.
opts: True
False
why: A forced first call, followed by later turns with automatic choice, guarantees the opening step such as metadata extraction.

q: Giving one agent eighteen tools generally improves selection reliability compared with giving it four or five.
opts: True
False
why: More tools raise decision complexity and lower selection accuracy. Specialized agents with small toolsets perform more reliably.

q: Requiring or forcing a tool call works with every model setting, including manual extended thinking.
opts: True
False
why: Documentation lists settings where these modes are rejected, for example manual extended thinking, so check support before relying on them. Automatic choice with strict tool use is the usual substitute.

q: A project-scoped .mcp.json file is intended to be committed to version control so that the team shares the same servers.
opts: True
False
why: That is its purpose. Personal or experimental servers belong in the user-level configuration instead.

q: Environment variable expansion in .mcp.json lets the file reference a token such as ${GITHUB_TOKEN} without storing the secret in the repository.
opts: True
False
why: The reference is resolved from each person's environment at load time, so the committed file contains no credential.

q: MCP resources are designed for performing actions with side effects, such as creating tickets.
opts: True
False
why: Resources expose read-only content for context. Actions with side effects are tools.

q: Glob searches the contents of files for a pattern.
opts: True
False
why: Glob matches file paths and names. Searching inside files is the job of a content search such as Grep.

q: A targeted edit requires the text being replaced to match exactly and to be unique in the file.
opts: True
False
why: If the text matches more than once, the edit fails, and the fix is a more specific anchor or reading the file and writing the updated content.

q: Reading every file in a repository first is the recommended way to start exploring an unfamiliar codebase.
opts: True
False
why: Build understanding incrementally: search for entry points, then read the files needed to follow imports and trace the flow.

q: A new engineer joins a team and finds that Claude Code ignores the team's naming conventions, although it follows them for everyone else. The conventions were added months ago by a senior developer who tested them locally. What is the most likely cause and the right fix?
opts: The conventions sit in the senior developer's user-level file; move them into the committed project instruction file
The new engineer must run /init once so that Claude downloads the conventions the team stored on a shared server
Instruction files expire after a few months, so the senior developer should re-save the conventions every quarter
Claude Code reads instructions only from the first prompt of a session, so the engineer should paste the full set of conventions into the first message of every new conversation
why: A user-level file applies only to its owner and never travels through version control, so only the senior developer's sessions see the conventions. The committed project file loads for anyone who works in the repository. The /init command generates a starter file rather than fetching shared rules, instruction files do not expire, and pasting rules into every conversation repeats work the project file exists to remove.

q: A project's instruction file has grown to about 600 lines covering API rules, testing rules, deployment steps and the history of past migrations. Claude increasingly ignores individual rules. Which restructuring is best?
opts: Add the word IMPORTANT in capitals to every rule so that each one stands out, and put the strictest rules first in the file
Prune what Claude can learn from the code and move area-specific conventions into small topic files under .claude/rules/, keeping only universal facts in the main file
Move the whole file into the user-level location so that it loads before any project content
Split the text into @-imported files and leave every line in place, since imported files add nothing to the context
why: Long files dilute adherence, so the fix is to cut what is derivable and scope the rest so it loads only when relevant. Emphasizing every line makes none of them stand out, a user-level file is neither shared nor smaller, and imports organize text but still load at launch, so they do not reduce context cost.

q: In a monorepo, the payments package must follow its own standards document and the web package a different one. Each package keeps a short instruction file. What is the cleanest way to give each package only the standards it needs?
opts: Paste both standards documents into the root instruction file so that every session starts with everything
Create one skill per package and remind developers to invoke the right one before they edit anything
In each package's instruction file, import the standards document that is relevant to that package using the at-path syntax
Put the payments standards in each payments developer's user-level file and the web standards in each web developer's, then ask them to keep those copies in sync by hand
why: Imports let each package's file pull in exactly the document its maintainers know is relevant, which keeps the setup modular and shared through version control. Pasting both documents at the root loads irrelevant standards everywhere, skills depend on people remembering to call them, and user-level files are personal copies that drift apart.

q: A developer wants Claude to remember her own sandbox URL and preferred test data for one repository, without sharing them with the team. Where should they go?
opts: In the committed project instruction file, under a heading that carries her name
In the user-level file in her home directory, which applies to this repository only
In a new file under .claude/rules/ so that teammates can choose to ignore it
In a CLAUDE.local.md file at the project root, which she adds to .gitignore
why: The local instruction file is read alongside the project file but is meant to stay out of version control, so it keeps personal, project-specific details private. A committed file or a rules file would be shared with the whole team, and the user-level file applies to every project on her machine, not just this repository.

q: Claude follows the logging convention in some sessions and not in others, and the team suspects that an instruction file is not being loaded where it should be. Which first step is best?
opts: Run /memory to see which instruction files are in play, then open them and look for gaps or conflicts
Reinstall Claude Code to clear its instruction cache, then restate the convention at the start of every prompt as a precaution
Ask Claude to recite its instructions and treat the answer as proof of which files were loaded
Copy the conventions into every developer's personal settings file so that each person maintains their own copy
why: The /memory command lists the instruction files that apply and lets you open them, which exposes missing or conflicting files; /context additionally shows what loaded at launch. Reinstalling changes nothing about where files live, Claude's own recital is not a reliable inventory, and personal copies make the inconsistency worse.

q: The team's instruction file says, in bold, never to edit anything under migrations/. Last week Claude edited a migration anyway. Which change gives a guarantee instead of a stronger request?
opts: Move the sentence to the top of the file and repeat it three times
Add a pre-tool hook, or a deny permission rule, that blocks writes to that folder
Put the sentence in the user-level file so that it loads before the project instructions
Turn the sentence into a skill that Claude is asked to run before every edit
why: Instruction files are context, not enforcement, so Claude can still overlook a rule. A hook or deny rule runs in the client and blocks the call whatever the model decides. Repeating or reordering text is still advisory, load order does not make a rule binding, and a skill is itself instructions that Claude may or may not follow.

q: A team keeps an instruction file in packages/api/ with API-specific rules. A developer starts Claude Code at the repository root and first asks about the web package only. What happens to the api file?
opts: It loads at launch together with the root file, since every instruction file in the tree is read up front
It replaces the root file for the session, because deeper files override shallower ones
It is not loaded at launch; it loads only when Claude reads or edits a file inside packages/api/, so it costs nothing until then
It is ignored unless the root file imports it with the at-path syntax
why: Instruction files below the working directory load on demand once Claude touches a file in that directory, so they cost nothing until they are relevant. Files in the working directory and its parents load at launch, files are combined rather than replaced, and no import is needed for on-demand loading.

q: Which two statements about the instruction-file hierarchy are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: The user-level file applies only to its owner and is not shared through version control
Imported files are fetched later, and only if Claude decides to ask for them
A project-level file that is committed to the repository gives every teammate the same instructions
Instruction files in subdirectories are all loaded at launch together with the root file
Files closer to the working directory override earlier files, so contradictory lines from parent directories are discarded
why: Scope decides who gets instructions: the user-level file stays personal, while the committed project file reaches everyone who clones the repository. Files are concatenated rather than overridden, so contradictions persist; subdirectory files load on demand; and imported files load at launch with the file that references them.

q: Which two practices keep a project instruction file effective? (Choose two.)
opts: Include long tutorials so that new engineers can read the file as well
Add a file-by-file description of the codebase so that Claude never needs to search
Write concrete, checkable instructions such as "use 2-space indentation"
Mark every rule as IMPORTANT to make sure none of them is skipped
Move multi-step procedures into skills and area-specific conventions into path-scoped rules
why: Short, specific, verifiable rules are followed more reliably, and moving procedural or area-specific material elsewhere keeps the always-loaded file small. Content Claude can derive from the code, tutorials and blanket emphasis all bloat the file and bury the rules that matter.

q: Instructions saved in the user-level file in your home directory are shared with your teammates through version control.
opts: True
False
why: That file lives outside the repository and applies only to you. To share instructions with the team, put them in the committed project-level file.

q: Splitting a large instruction file into imported files makes it better organized but does not reduce how much context it uses.
opts: True
False
why: Imported files are expanded and loaded at launch together with the file that references them. Reducing context cost takes pruning or path-scoped rules.

q: If an instruction file says that a command is forbidden, Claude Code blocks that command.
opts: True
False
why: Instruction files are delivered as context, so Claude may follow the rule but nothing enforces it. Blocking requires a permission deny rule or a hook.

q: A /release-notes workflow reads dozens of merged pull requests and prints thousands of lines of intermediate text that clutter the developer's session. What is the best way to configure it?
opts: Move its steps into the root instruction file so that Claude follows them quietly in every session without printing anything
Set disable-model-invocation to true, which shortens the output that the skill produces
List the git commands in allowed-tools so that their output is truncated
Make it a skill with context set to fork, so the work runs in an isolated subagent and only the result returns
why: A forked skill runs in its own context, so intermediate output never enters the main conversation. Moving the steps into the instruction file loads them every session and isolates nothing, disable-model-invocation only controls who may start the skill, and allowed-tools pre-approves tools without shortening what they print.

q: A /deploy skill pushes to production. The team worries that Claude might start a deployment on its own because the code looks ready. Which setting prevents that?
opts: disable-model-invocation set to true, so the skill runs only when a person invokes it
context set to fork, so that the deployment runs in an isolated subagent that cannot reach the production environment
An argument-hint naming the target environment, so that Claude must ask before it deploys
A line in the instruction file asking Claude to wait for approval before any deployment
why: That field removes Claude's ability to load the skill by itself, so only an explicit command starts it. Forking changes where the work runs, not who may start it; an argument hint is just an autocomplete prompt; and a sentence in the instruction file is advisory and can be overlooked.

q: A /commit skill should be able to run git add, git status and git commit without a permission prompt each time it runs, while every other tool keeps its normal approval behavior. What should the skill declare?
opts: context set to fork, which gives forked skills unrestricted use of Bash and every other tool without prompts
allowed-tools in its frontmatter, listing Bash(git add *), Bash(git status *) and Bash(git commit *)
An argument-hint listing the three git commands so that developers know they are permitted
bypassPermissions in the root instruction file, scoped to the commit workflow
why: The allowed-tools field pre-approves the listed tool patterns for the turn in which the skill runs, which is exactly "no prompt for these, normal rules for everything else". Forking does not grant tools, an argument hint is a display string, and a permission mode is a session setting that an instruction file cannot switch.

q: A team has two pieces of guidance: "always use pnpm and run the typecheck before finishing", and a twelve-step release checklist used about twice a month. Where should each live?
opts: Both in the project instruction file, so that nothing is ever forgotten, even rarely used steps
Both as skills, to keep the always-loaded context as small as possible
The universal rule in the instruction file, the checklist in a skill invoked on demand
The universal rule in a skill, and the checklist in the project instruction file
why: Always-true standards belong in the file that loads every session, while a rarely used multi-step procedure should cost context only when needed, which is what a skill does. Putting both in the file wastes context on the checklist, putting both in skills risks the universal rule not being applied, and the reverse assignment gets both wrong.

q: A developer wants a personal version of the team's /review skill that also checks accessibility, without changing what her teammates get. What is the best approach?
opts: Edit the committed project skill and tell teammates to ignore the accessibility step
Add accessibility rules to the project instruction file so that every review includes them
Set disable-model-invocation on the project skill and re-create the workflow locally
Copy the skill into her personal skills folder in the home directory under a new name and extend it there
why: A personal skill lives outside the repository, so it affects nobody else, and a distinct name avoids confusion with the shared one. Editing the committed skill or the project instruction file changes behavior for the whole team, and changing the shared skill's frontmatter changes how it is triggered for everyone.

q: A skill with context set to fork returns almost nothing useful. Its entire body reads: "Use kebab-case for URL paths and camelCase for JSON properties." What is the most likely reason?
opts: The forked subagent got guidelines but no task, so it has nothing to do; reference content belongs in an inline skill
Forked skills cannot read bodies longer than a single sentence, so the text was truncated
The subagent needs the full conversation history, which forking always supplies, to interpret guidelines like these correctly
The skill has no name field, so the forked run was never started
why: A forked skill's body becomes the subagent's prompt, so it must describe a task. Guidelines belong in an inline skill or the instruction file, where they shape the work in the main conversation. The subagent does not receive the conversation history, and a missing name falls back to the directory name rather than stopping the run.

q: A forked research skill must never be able to edit files. Which configuration fits best?
opts: Set allowed-tools to Read, Grep and Glob, which removes every other tool from the run for as long as the skill is active
Point the skill's agent field at the built-in Explore subagent, whose tools are read-only
Add "never modify files" to the skill body and rely on the instruction
Set disable-model-invocation to true so that the skill can run only when requested
why: Explore's tool set excludes Write and Edit, so the restriction is structural. In current docs allowed-tools only pre-approves tools and leaves the rest available (disallowed-tools or a restricted agent type is what removes them); a sentence in the body is advisory; and disable-model-invocation controls who can start the skill, not what it can do once running.

q: Developers often run /fix-issue with no argument and get a confused answer, because the skill expects an issue number. What is the best improvement?
opts: Rename the skill to fix-issue-number so that the requirement is obvious from its name
Set context to fork so that the subagent asks the user for the missing number
Add an argument-hint such as [issue-number] and use $ARGUMENTS in the body where the number belongs
List Bash(gh *) in allowed-tools so that the skill can run the GitHub CLI and look up the right issue number itself
why: The hint appears during autocomplete and tells the developer which argument is expected, and $ARGUMENTS passes whatever they type into the instructions. Renaming does not prompt anyone, forking does not ask for input, and pre-approving the GitHub CLI does not tell the skill which issue is meant.

q: Which two statements about skill frontmatter are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: argument-hint rejects an invocation that is missing a required argument
allowed-tools removes every tool that is not listed for as long as the session lasts
context set to fork runs the skill in an isolated subagent that does not see the conversation history
A misspelled field name stops the skill from loading and reports an error
disable-model-invocation set to true means the skill runs only when a person invokes it
why: Forking isolates the run, and disabling model invocation reserves the skill for people. The allowed-tools field only pre-approves listed tools for the turn, the hint is a display string that validates nothing, and unrecognized fields are ignored without an error.

q: Which two belong in a skill rather than in the always-loaded instruction file? (Choose two.)
opts: A workflow for drafting a pull-request description from the current diff, invoked on request
The team's branch-naming convention
The rule that all code uses two-space indentation
The command used to run the project's tests
A multi-step procedure for preparing a release, run only occasionally
why: Skills load on demand, so they suit task-specific, occasional workflows. Test commands, formatting rules and branch naming apply broadly and cost little, so they belong in the file that loads every session.

q: By default, a skill's description is available so that Claude can decide when to use it, while the skill's full instructions load only when it is invoked.
opts: True
False
why: That split is why skills cost little context until used. A skill with disable-model-invocation set to true is the exception, because its description is not offered to Claude.

q: A command file saved in the .claude/commands/ folder of your home directory is shared with every developer who clones the repository.
opts: True
False
why: The home-directory folder is personal and never travels with the repository. Team-wide commands go in the project's own .claude/commands/ folder, which is committed.

q: In current Claude Code, a skill's allowed-tools field pre-approves the listed tools for that turn but does not stop Claude from using other tools, which stay subject to the normal permission rules.
opts: True
False
why: The exam guide describes the field as a way to limit a skill's tools, but the current documentation is explicit that it grants approval. Removing tools takes disallowed-tools, deny rules or a restricted agent type.

q: GraphQL schema files ending in .graphql sit in a dozen service folders, and all of them must follow one set of naming conventions. Developers working on other files should not load these conventions. What is the most maintainable approach?
opts: A separate instruction file in each of the twelve service folders, repeating the same conventions
A section in the root instruction file that Claude is expected to apply only when it meets a schema file
A skill that developers invoke by name whenever they open a schema file
One rule file under .claude/rules/ whose paths field matches the .graphql extension in any directory of the repository
why: A glob in a path-scoped rule follows the file type wherever it lives and loads only for matching files. Twelve copies are hard to keep consistent, a root-file section loads for everyone all the time and relies on inference, and a skill depends on a person remembering to call it.

q: A rule file was meant to apply only to TypeScript API handlers, but Claude seems to load it even when editing the README. The author recalls typing the frontmatter by hand. What is the most plausible explanation?
opts: The paths frontmatter is missing or not valid YAML, so the rule is unconditional and loads for all work
Rules always load for every file in the project, regardless of any frontmatter
Glob patterns are not supported in rule files, so Claude Code falls back to loading every rule for every file it touches
Rule files must be named after the directory they target, and this file's name does not match
why: A rule without a usable paths field is unconditional, and malformed YAML is ignored so the rule loads as if it had no paths. Rules with valid paths load only for matching files, globs are the supported mechanism, and rule file names are free-form topic names.

q: A root instruction file lists React, API, database and Terraform conventions. A developer who is only editing CSS notices that context fills quickly and responses seem less focused. Which change addresses the cause best?
opts: Keep everything in the root file but add a sentence telling Claude to ignore conventions for other areas
Move each area's conventions into rule files with paths, so they load only when matching files are read or edited
Import all four convention documents with the at-path syntax so that they are organized separately
Move the conventions into that developer's user-level file so that only she pays the context cost
why: Path-scoped rules keep irrelevant conventions out of context. Telling Claude to ignore text does not remove its token cost, imported files load at launch just like the original text, and a user-level file would still load in all of her projects while hiding the team's standards from everyone else.

q: After a long session and a compaction, Claude stops applying a path-scoped rule until it opens another file that matches. The rule must hold at all times. What should the team do?
opts: Ask Claude after every compaction to re-read the rules directory
Raise the compaction threshold so that long conversations are never summarized and the rule always stays in context
Drop the paths field, or move the rule into the root instruction file, so it loads unconditionally
Convert the rule into a skill that developers invoke at the start of each task
why: Path-scoped rules enter the conversation when a matching file is touched, so summarizing can fold them away, whereas unconditional rules and the root file are re-injected from disk. Manual reminders are error-prone, long work cannot avoid compaction, and a skill depends on someone invoking it and is itself subject to compaction budgets.

q: Which situation is best served by a directory-level instruction file rather than a path-scoped rule?
opts: A naming convention for every test file in the monorepo, wherever those files sit in the directory tree
Formatting rules for all Terraform and YAML files across the monorepo
Rules for any file whose name ends in .generated.ts, in any folder
Conventions for everything inside one package directory, such as packages/billing, and nothing else
why: A directory file is bound to its folder, so it fits conventions that belong to a single package. The other three follow a file type or name pattern across many directories, which is the case for glob patterns in path-scoped rules.

q: Which two statements about path-scoped rules are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: A rule file with no paths field loads at launch and applies to all work
They load for the whole session as soon as any file in the repository is opened
Claude Code enforces them, so Claude cannot violate a loaded rule
The paths field accepts a single literal directory name and no glob syntax
They load when Claude reads, writes or edits a file that matches one of the glob patterns
why: Matching a file triggers loading, and the absence of paths makes a rule unconditional. The field takes glob patterns, a loaded rule is still an instruction rather than enforcement, and loading is tied to matching files, not to opening any file.

q: A path-scoped rule is a better fit than a subdirectory instruction file when the same convention must apply to files of one type spread across many directories.
opts: True
False
why: A directory file covers only its own folder, whereas a glob in a rule follows the file type wherever it appears.

q: Each file in .claude/rules/ must be named after the directory it applies to.
opts: True
False
why: Rule files are named for their topic, such as testing or api-design. Their scope comes from the optional paths field, not from the file name.

q: A bug report includes a stack trace that points to one function in one file: a date string is parsed without checking for an empty value. What is the best way to handle the fix in Claude Code?
opts: Ask Claude to make the fix directly and run the relevant test
Enter plan mode first, since every change should be planned and approved before any edit is made
Delegate the fix to the Explore subagent, which will locate and repair the function in its own context
Start with the interview pattern so that Claude can ask about every possible date format in the system
why: The scope is small and well understood, so direct execution is quickest and cheapest. Planning overhead pays off for uncertain, multi-file or architectural work. Explore is read-only and cannot edit, and an interview is for unfamiliar design territory, not a one-line empty-value check.

q: A product needs real-time notifications. The team can use WebSockets, server-sent events or polling, and each option needs different infrastructure and touches many modules. How should the developer start in Claude Code?
opts: Pick the simplest option, begin implementing it directly, and revisit the choice if problems appear later
Use plan mode to explore the codebase and compare the approaches before any code is changed
Write exhaustive instructions for the WebSocket design and run them in direct execution mode
Ask Claude to implement all three approaches in parallel and keep whichever one passes the tests first
why: Several valid approaches with different infrastructure needs is the textbook case for plan mode: explore, compare and design before committing. Starting to implement risks costly rework, detailed upfront instructions assume the answer is already known, and building all three multiplies the effort without resolving the decision.

q: A developer must understand how authentication works across a large, unfamiliar service before changing it. Reading dozens of files in the main conversation would fill the context. What is the best approach?
opts: Read every authentication-related file in the main conversation first so nothing is missed, then run /clear before editing
Skip exploration and let Claude infer the design from the first error message that appears during implementation
Have the Explore subagent investigate and return a summary, so that the file reads stay in its own context
Turn off plan mode so that Claude can explore the code faster without waiting for any approval
why: Explore works in a separate, read-only context and returns only its findings, which preserves the main conversation for the actual change. Reading everything in the main thread is what fills the window, and /clear would throw away what was learned. Guessing from an error skips discovery, and plan mode does not slow exploration; it only withholds edits.

q: A team must upgrade a major library version that affects about 45 files, with several deprecated patterns that each need a different replacement. Which workflow is best?
opts: Edit the files one by one in direct mode and replan only if the tests start failing partway through
Stay in plan mode for the entire task, including the edits, because plan mode is the safest mode available
Hand the edits to the Explore subagent so that they happen outside the main conversation and cost no context
Plan first to survey usages and design the migration, then approve the plan and carry it out directly
why: A large migration with several patterns benefits from a survey-and-design phase, after which the approved plan is executed in the same session. Incremental editing without a plan invites rework when later patterns surface, plan mode makes no source edits until a plan is approved, and Explore is read-only.

q: A manager asks the team to use plan mode for every task, while a developer finds it overkill for renaming a variable. Which guidance is best?
opts: Plan when the approach is uncertain, the change spans several files or the code is unfamiliar; make small, clear changes directly
Always plan, because planning costs nothing and prevents every kind of rework, whatever the size of the change
Never plan, because code review will catch any mistakes after the change has been made
Plan only when more than ten files are involved, since file count is the one reliable signal of risk
why: Planning adds overhead that pays off when scope or approach is uncertain. A useful test is whether you could describe the diff in one sentence; if so, skip the plan. Always planning wastes effort on trivial edits, never planning invites rework on architectural changes, and a fixed file-count threshold ignores how unclear or risky a change is.

q: In plan mode Claude proposes a plan that mostly fits, but the developer disagrees with one design choice. What is the best way to proceed?
opts: Approve the plan as written and correct the disputed choice with follow-up prompts once the code exists
Edit the plan or tell Claude what to change and keep planning, then approve the revised plan
Leave plan mode and rewrite the whole task from scratch as a single direct-execution prompt
Clear the conversation and start over, because plans cannot be changed once they have been presented
why: The approval step exists so that you can shape the plan before any code changes: open it in an editor, change it, or ask for revisions. Approving a flawed plan commits to rework, discarding the exploration wastes it, and plans are not frozen once presented.

q: Which two tasks are best suited to plan mode? (Choose two.)
opts: Restructuring a module whose callers are spread across dozens of files
Choosing between two integration approaches that need different infrastructure
Renaming a local variable inside one method
Adding a single log line to one function
Fixing a typo in a README paragraph
why: Plan mode pays off for architectural decisions and large multi-file changes, where early exploration prevents rework. The other three are tiny, well-scoped edits that direct execution handles in seconds.

q: Which two statements about the Explore subagent are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: It inherits the full conversation history of the main session when it starts
Its verbose discovery output stays in a separate context window and a summary returns to the main conversation
It must be defined in the project's agents folder before it can be used
It is read-only, so Write and Edit are denied
It can modify files when it is asked to be very thorough in its search
why: Explore is a built-in, read-only agent that does its searching in its own context and reports back. Thoroughness levels change how deeply it searches, not what it may write; it starts fresh rather than inheriting history; and it needs no definition file because it ships with Claude Code.

q: Plan mode lets Claude explore the codebase and propose an approach without editing source files until the developer approves the plan.
opts: True
False
why: Exploring and designing first is the purpose of plan mode, which is why it suits large or uncertain changes.

q: Direct execution is appropriate for a well-understood, narrowly scoped change such as adding one validation check to a function.
opts: True
False
why: When the scope is clear and small, a separate planning phase adds overhead without reducing risk.

q: The Explore subagent works inside the main conversation's context window, so everything it reads counts against that window.
opts: True
False
why: Explore runs in its own context window and returns a summary, which is the reason to use it for verbose discovery.

q: A script that normalizes customer phone numbers keeps producing different formats for the same kinds of input, even after a three-paragraph description of the desired output. What is the best next step?
opts: Rewrite the description with stronger wording and capital letters on the key requirements
Run the script ten times and ask Claude to keep whichever format appears most often
Add two or three before-and-after examples, including a messy input and the exact result wanted
Switch to plan mode so that Claude can reason about the formats before it edits the script
why: Concrete input and output pairs remove the ambiguity that prose leaves, and they carry edge cases along. A longer or louder description is still open to the same misreading, majority voting does not define the right format, and plan mode helps with design uncertainty rather than inconsistent interpretation.

q: A developer must build a feature in an area she has never worked in: a cache with invalidation rules. She is not sure what to ask. Which approach best surfaces the considerations she has not thought of?
opts: Ask Claude to implement the first design that comes to mind and review the resulting diff afterwards
Write a complete specification alone before involving Claude, to avoid influencing its answers
Ask for a single paragraph describing cache invalidation, then implement directly from that paragraph
Have Claude interview her about requirements, failure modes and tradeoffs, then write a spec before implementing
why: In unfamiliar territory the interview pattern turns Claude's questions into a checklist of design considerations, such as invalidation strategies and failure modes, before any code exists. Implementing first bakes in untested assumptions, writing the spec alone repeats her blind spots, and a generic paragraph does not probe her situation.

q: A data-migration script crashes on rows that contain null values in a legacy column. What is the most effective way to get a robust fix?
opts: Give Claude a concrete failing case, an input row with a null and the output expected, and ask it to fix the script and run it
Describe in prose that the script should "handle missing data gracefully" and let Claude decide what that means
Ask Claude to wrap the whole migration in a catch-all error handler so that it can never crash
Remove every row that contains a null from the input before running the migration
why: A specific example with expected output pins down the intended behavior and gives Claude something to verify against. A vague phrase invites guesses, a catch-all handler hides failures instead of defining the correct result, and deleting rows silently loses data.

q: A pricing module has three bugs: rounding errors, a wrong currency-conversion order, and discounts that stack incorrectly. Fixing any one of them changes the results of the others. How should the developer report them?
opts: Report them one per message in order of severity so that each fix can be reviewed in isolation from the rest
Describe all three in one detailed message so that Claude can design fixes that account for how they interact
Open three parallel sessions, one per bug, and merge the resulting changes at the end of the day
Ask Claude to fix the easiest bug first and mention the others only if the tests start failing
why: When problems interact, sequential fixes can undo or invalidate one another, so one message that explains the whole picture lets Claude plan a consistent solution. Separate messages or sessions hide the dependencies and risk conflicting changes.

q: A developer has corrected Claude three times about the same misunderstanding, and its answers keep drifting back. The session is long and full of discarded attempts. What is the best move?
opts: Keep correcting, using stronger wording and more capital letters each time the mistake reappears
Compact the conversation and continue, since the summary will keep only what is useful
Clear the session and start again with a more specific prompt that includes what was learned
Switch to a different permission mode so that Claude pays closer attention to the corrections
why: After repeated failed corrections the context is cluttered with wrong approaches, and a fresh session with a sharper prompt usually outperforms patching. Compaction would carry the clutter forward in summary form, emphasis does not fix a misunderstanding, and permission modes do not affect attention.

q: Claude reported that a new CSV importer was finished, but it breaks on fields that contain quoted commas. Which change best prevents this in future tasks?
opts: Ask Claude to review its own work carefully before it says that it is done
Tell Claude to be more careful about edge cases at the start of every prompt
Read every diff by hand before accepting any change from Claude
Provide runnable verification, such as tests with representative inputs including quoted fields, and have Claude run them until they pass
why: A check Claude can run closes the loop, so it keeps working until the evidence says the job is right. Asking for care or self-review relies on the same judgment that missed the case, and reading every diff by hand does not scale and leaves you as the verification loop.

q: A team wants Claude to implement a rate limiter with specific burst and refill behavior. Which workflow most reliably produces a correct implementation?
opts: Write tests for the expected behavior, edge cases and performance first, then have Claude implement and iterate on the failures
Have Claude write both the limiter and its tests in a single pass, then trust the passing result
Describe the burst and refill behavior in detail and verify the implementation by reading the code
Ask Claude to implement the limiter now and add tests only after users report problems
why: Tests written first define the target independently of the implementation, and sharing failures steers each iteration. Letting Claude write both in one pass can encode the same misunderstanding in code and tests, reading code is a weaker check than running it, and adding tests after complaints comes too late.

q: Which two actions fit test-driven iteration with Claude Code? (Choose two.)
opts: Ask Claude to delete tests it considers redundant before it starts
Disable a failing test temporarily so that Claude can finish the feature
Write tests that cover expected behavior and edge cases before the implementation exists
Describe failures in general terms to avoid anchoring Claude on one case
Paste the failing test output back to Claude after each attempt
why: Tests first and failures shared back are the two halves of the loop: a target, then concrete feedback. Disabling tests, vague failure descriptions and letting Claude prune tests all weaken the signal the loop depends on.

q: When several bugs interact, describing them together in one detailed message is generally better than fixing them one at a time.
opts: True
False
why: Fixes to interacting problems can invalidate each other, so Claude needs the whole picture. Independent problems, by contrast, can be handled one after another.

q: In the interview pattern, the developer must write a complete specification before Claude is allowed to ask any questions.
opts: True
False
why: The pattern is the reverse: Claude asks questions first to surface considerations the developer may have missed, and the answers become the spec.

q: A CI step posts Claude's review as inline pull-request comments by parsing the prose with regular expressions, and it breaks whenever the wording changes. What is the best fix?
opts: Tell Claude to always write findings in one fixed sentence template and keep the regular expressions
Run in print mode with JSON output and a schema for the findings, then read the structured_output field
Switch to streaming output and parse the individual tokens as they arrive from the model
Run the review twice and post only those findings whose wording matches in both runs
why: A schema-constrained result gives the pipeline machine-readable fields such as file, line and severity, so wording no longer matters. A template is still free text, token-level parsing is even more fragile, and comparing wording across two runs only discards findings.

q: In a pipeline, the same Claude session that wrote a feature is then asked to review it before merge. Its reviews rarely find anything. What is the best change?
opts: Tell the same session to take a more critical stance and to look harder for problems
Ask the same session to think for longer before it approves its own change
Run the review in a separate, fresh invocation that sees only the diff and the criteria
Run the same session's review twice and require both runs to find the same issues
why: A session that wrote the code still holds its own reasoning and tends to defend its decisions, whereas an independent instance questions them. Instructions to be critical, extra thinking time and repeated self-review do not remove that bias.

q: After every new commit to a pull request, the review job posts the same nine comments again plus one new one, and developers have started to ignore the bot. What is the best change?
opts: Delete all of the bot's earlier comments before each run and then post the complete list again
Run the review only when the pull request is merged instead of on each commit
Ask Claude to shorten each comment so that the repeated ones take up less space
Include the earlier findings in the prompt and tell Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues
why: The model does not remember the previous run, so the pipeline must supply the earlier findings and ask for only what is new or unresolved. Deleting and reposting still repeats everything, moving the review to merge time loses the feedback loop, and shorter comments leave the duplication in place.

q: A CI job that generates test suggestions keeps proposing scenarios the suite already covers. What is the best fix?
opts: Provide the existing test files in the context and tell Claude to avoid scenarios they already cover
Ask for fewer suggestions per run so that the duplicates are less noticeable to reviewers
Run the job less often so that developers see fewer repeated suggestions over the month
Cap the number of turns for each run so that Claude stops earlier and proposes less
why: Claude cannot avoid duplicates it cannot see, so the existing tests must be in context. Asking for fewer suggestions, running less often or capping turns only hides the symptom.

q: Tests generated in CI are trivial, such as getters and framework behavior, and they ignore the project's fixtures. The job runs claude -p inside the repository. Which change is most effective?
opts: Add the phrase "write high-quality tests" to the end of every CI prompt
Document the testing standards, what makes a test worth writing, and the available fixtures in the project's instruction file
Generate three times as many tests and discard those that do not increase coverage
Move the job to the Message Batches API so that the model has more time to think per test
why: The instruction file is how project context reaches a non-interactive run, so recording the standards, the criteria for valuable tests and the fixtures steers generation. A generic quality request adds no information, filtering by coverage keeps trivial tests that still raise coverage, and batch processing changes cost and latency, not guidance.

q: A nightly job on a shared runner that holds production credentials runs claude -p to fix lint errors, and runs sometimes end early because a step the job needs was never pre-approved. What is the best configuration?
opts: Run with bypassPermissions so that nothing can ever prompt, since the job is unattended anyway
Pipe the word "yes" into the job's standard input so that every prompt is accepted
Pre-approve the exact tools needed with --allowedTools and use dontAsk mode so that anything else is denied
Add "do not ask for permission" to the prompt text so that Claude proceeds without waiting
why: The allowed list pre-approves what the task needs, and dontAsk makes every other action a plain denial, so the policy is explicit and nothing waits for a prompt that no one can answer. Bypassing all checks on a runner with production credentials is unsafe, because that mode is meant for isolated environments; piped input does not reliably answer permission dialogs; and prompt text cannot switch permission behavior off.

q: A team wants Claude to review every pull request automatically when it is opened, without anyone mentioning @claude. How should the GitHub Action step be configured?
opts: Leave the prompt empty, because the action reviews every pull request on its own once it is installed
Ask developers to comment @claude on each pull request so that the action wakes up and starts
Raise the maximum number of turns so that the action keeps listening for newly opened pull requests
Give the action a prompt input that describes the review, and trigger the workflow on pull-request events
why: With a prompt input the action runs in automation mode on whatever event triggers the workflow. Without a prompt it waits for the trigger phrase, so an empty prompt reviews nothing, relying on manual mentions defeats the automation, and a turn limit has nothing to do with triggering.

q: Reviews in CI began ignoring the project's conventions after the team added --bare to the claude -p command for reproducibility. What explains this, and what is the fix?
opts: Bare mode skips automatic loading of instruction files, so the guidance must be passed explicitly, for example with --append-system-prompt-file
Print mode never reads instruction files, so the conventions must be moved into the settings file instead
Bare mode disables the model's ability to follow instructions, so the flag should be removed permanently
Instruction files are read only from the home directory in CI, so they must be copied there first
why: Bare mode skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and instruction files so that runs are reproducible, and context must then be supplied through flags such as an appended system prompt file. Without bare mode, print mode loads the project's instruction file as usual.

q: A team's committed .claude/settings.json sets the default model for the repository. One developer prefers a different model in this repository only and does not want to commit a change. Where should she put the override?
opts: In ~/.claude/settings.json, because user settings always override project settings
In .claude/settings.local.json, which ranks above the shared project file and stays out of version control
In the committed .claude/settings.json, then ask teammates to override it back if they disagree
In CLAUDE.local.md, since it is also a personal file that sits next to the project settings
why: The project-local settings file sits above the shared project file in precedence and is kept out of git, so only her sessions change. User settings rank below project settings, editing the committed file changes it for everyone, and a CLAUDE.local.md file holds instructions for Claude, not settings.

q: A project's settings contain a deny rule for Bash(aws *) and, from another file, an allow rule for Bash(aws s3 ls). What happens when Claude tries to run aws s3 ls?
opts: The call runs, because the narrower allow rule is more specific than the broad deny
The call runs only if the user's settings file sets the allow rule, since user rules outrank project rules
The call is blocked, because deny rules are evaluated before allow rules and the first match decides
Claude Code asks for confirmation each time, because the two rules cancel each other out
why: Rules are checked in the order deny, ask, allow, and the first match wins, so a broad deny cannot be carved out by a narrower allow. Specificity does not change the order, file origin does not make an allow outrank a deny, and the rules do not cancel.

q: Which two practices help CI-invoked Claude Code generate useful tests? (Choose two.)
opts: Ask for the largest possible number of tests to maximize coverage
Let the job pause for interactive approval before each test file is written
Document the project's testing standards and available fixtures where the run can read them
Provide the existing test files so that suggestions avoid scenarios already covered
Strip out all project context so that every run starts from an identical blank state
why: Seeing what already exists and knowing the conventions are what make suggestions new and fitting. Maximizing quantity produces low-value tests, interactive pauses stall an unattended job, and removing context removes exactly the information needed.

q: Which two statements about running Claude Code in a pipeline are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: The --ci flag switches Claude Code to the Message Batches API at half price
When no terminal is attached, permission prompts are approved automatically so that the run can finish
Setting CLAUDE_NONINTERACTIVE=1 is the documented way to avoid hangs
With --output-format json and --json-schema, the structured result is returned in the structured_output field
The -p flag runs a single prompt non-interactively, prints the result and exits
why: Print mode and the structured-output flags are documented, parseable pipeline features. The other three describe things that do not exist or that Claude Code does not do: there is no such flag or variable, and a permission request nobody can answer is denied unless it was pre-approved, never approved automatically.

q: A session that generated code is just as effective at reviewing its own changes as a fresh, independent Claude instance.
opts: True
False
why: The generating session retains its own reasoning and is less likely to question its decisions. An independent instance reviewing only the diff and criteria catches subtler issues.

q: When a review is rerun after new commits, including the earlier findings in the prompt and asking for only new or unresolved issues reduces duplicate comments.
opts: True
False
why: The model does not remember the previous run, so the pipeline has to supply the earlier findings.

q: Running Claude Code with --bare skips automatic loading of CLAUDE.md, so project guidance must then be supplied another way.
opts: True
False
why: Bare mode skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and instruction files. Pass what you need with flags such as an appended system prompt file.

q: Your team's pull-request bot reviews Python services for security problems. Its prompt ends with: "Only report issues you are highly confident are real vulnerabilities." Engineers still get many warnings about harmless code, such as parameterized queries and input validated upstream, and have started ignoring the bot. Which change is most likely to improve precision?
opts: Strengthen the wording to "only report issues you are 95% certain are exploitable", so the model applies a much higher bar before it speaks up
Have the model attach a confidence score between 0 and 1 to every warning and let code drop any warning scoring below 0.8
Define what to report (string-built SQL, hard-coded secrets, missing authorization checks) and what to skip (parameterized queries, validated input)
Switch to the largest available model, which should be better at telling harmless code from real vulnerabilities in a large service
why: A request for confidence adds no decision boundary: the model already believes the findings it makes, so a stronger phrase or a score cutoff changes little, and self-reported confidence is not calibrated precision. Defining what counts as reportable and what to skip changes the decision itself. A larger model still does not know your team's definition of a reportable issue.

q: A CI job asks Claude to "check that the README examples are accurate". Its comments are full of complaints about wording, missing detail and tone, and maintainers now skim past them. Which rewritten instruction should cut the noise most?
opts: Flag an example only when running it as written would fail or print something different from what the README shows
Check each example carefully, but be conservative and avoid nitpicking about wording, tone or missing detail
Rate every example from 1 to 10 for accuracy and report only the examples that score below 5
Flag any example that a first-time user could plausibly find confusing, and sort the flags by importance before posting them
why: Flagging an example only when running it would fail is a test the model can answer yes or no, so the bar no longer depends on its own taste. "Accurate" and "conservative" leave the bar undefined, a numeric rating only moves that ambiguity into a number, and "confusing" widens the net to exactly the wording complaints you want to drop.

q: Your review assistant posts findings in four categories. After a month, measured precision is 93% for security, 88% for bugs, 31% for performance and 22% for naming. Developers have begun dismissing every finding unread, including the security ones. What should you do first?
opts: Keep all four categories running and add a banner saying that some findings may be wrong, so developers read each one carefully
