Segments that pass can be automated while the failing one stays under review. Dropping review everywhere would let about a third of handwritten forms through wrong, demanding perfection is impractical, and a flat random sample is dominated by easy typed invoices, so it would barely see the problem.

q: A team auto-approves every extraction with a confidence above 0.9 and no longer reviews them. Three months later a supplier changes its invoice layout, and the resulting errors go unnoticed until a customer complains. Which practice would have caught the problem earlier?
opts: Review every extraction rated above 0.9 as well, so that nothing in the pipeline is automated any more
Lower the auto-approval threshold from 0.9 to 0.8 so that a larger share of documents is reviewed by people
Review a stratified random sample of the auto-approved extractions every week and track errors by segment
Ask the model to explain, for every extraction it approves, why it is confident in the values it extracted
why: Automation removes the checking that would reveal a new failure pattern. Regular stratified random sampling of high-confidence outputs keeps measuring their true error rate by segment, such as supplier or document type, and surfaces new patterns like a layout change. Reviewing everything defeats the purpose of automating, a lower threshold still trusts the model's confidence on layouts it misreads, and a self-explanation is not an independent measurement.

q: An extraction prompt now asks the model to report a confidence score for each field. How should the team choose the thresholds that decide which fields go to human review?
opts: Use 0.9 for every field, because that is the conventional cut-off for high confidence in extraction work
Ask the model to justify its scores and set each threshold where the justification sounds convincing enough
Copy the thresholds from another team's pipeline, since confidence scores mean the same thing everywhere
Calibrate against a labeled validation set and set thresholds from how often each field is right at each level
why: A raw score is only the model's opinion. It becomes a routing signal once it is checked against labeled data: if fields scored 0.9 are right nine times in ten, then 0.9 means something. A conventional cut-off, a persuasive justification and borrowed thresholds all skip that measurement, and scores differ by model, prompt, field and document mix.

q: Reviewers can check about 500 extractions per day, but 1,200 land in the review queue. Which prioritization makes the best use of reviewer time?
opts: Review in order of arrival until the day's capacity is used, so that no document waits longer than another
Review the lowest calibrated confidence first, with documents whose sources conflict or are ambiguous
Review a random 500 each day, so that every document has an equal chance of being checked by a person
Review the largest documents first, since they contain the most fields that could be wrong in them
why: With limited capacity, reviewers should see the extractions most likely to be wrong first: low calibrated confidence, or ambiguous or contradictory source documents. Arrival order and random selection ignore risk, and size is a weak proxy for it. A separate stratified sample of confident outputs still runs alongside to catch what the scores miss.

q: Two documents attached to the same insurance claim state different dates of loss. The extraction model outputs one of the dates with a confidence of 0.96. What should the pipeline do?
opts: Accept the date, since 0.96 is above the review threshold and the pipeline can send the claim straight on
Reject the claim automatically and ask the customer to resubmit documents that are consistent with each other
Route the claim to human review, because the sources contradict each other whatever the confidence
Keep the date from the document that was uploaded most recently, as it is probably the corrected one
why: Contradictory or ambiguous sources belong with a person: a high score cannot settle a disagreement between documents, and choosing either date is a guess. Accepting by score, choosing by upload time or rejecting automatically each skip the human judgement that the conflict needs.

q: A team wants to know whether it is safe to expand the automated acceptance of extractions. Which two measures give the most reliable evidence? (Choose two.)
opts: A single overall accuracy figure computed across every document
Accuracy broken down by document type and by field on a labeled set
Accuracy measured only on the extractions that the model scored as low confidence
The model's own written assessment of how reliable its extractions have been
Ongoing review of stratified random samples of the high-confidence extractions
why: Per-segment accuracy reveals the weak document types and fields that an average hides, and ongoing stratified sampling measures the true error rate among the outputs that automation no longer checks while exposing new patterns. An overall figure masks weak segments, sampling only low-confidence items says nothing about the confident ones being accepted, and self-assessment is not independent evidence.

q: A 97% overall accuracy figure shows that every document type and every field is also close to 97% accurate.
opts: True
False
why: An overall number is an average weighted by volume, so a large, easy segment can hide a small, weak one. Accuracy has to be checked by document type and field before human review is reduced.

q: Stratified random sampling draws samples separately from each segment, such as each document type, so that small segments are represented in the measurement of error rates.
opts: True
False
why: Sampling within each stratum guarantees that rare but important segments are checked, which a single pooled random sample might skip. It supports ongoing error-rate measurement and the detection of new failure patterns.

q: Two credible sources report different 30-day readmission rates for heart-failure patients: a national registry says 21% and an insurer's claims analysis says 24%. What should the synthesis agent do?
opts: Report the registry's figure alone, because registries are generally regarded as more authoritative sources
Report the average, 22.5%, as the best single estimate of the true readmission rate for these patients
Report both figures, each labeled with its source and, if known, its method, and flag that they differ
Leave the statistic out of the report altogether, because the sources disagree about what the rate is
why: When credible sources conflict, the honest output keeps both values with attribution, so the reader can weigh them; differences often come from definitions, populations or years. Silently choosing one hides the disagreement, an average is a number that no source reported, and omitting the statistic discards useful evidence.

q: A synthesis agent flags a "contradiction": one source says 12% of firms use a technology, another says 31%. The 12% figure comes from a 2021 survey and the 31% figure from a 2025 survey, but the subagents' outputs did not show dates. Which change best prevents false contradictions like this?
opts: Require subagents to include the publication or data-collection date in each structured finding
Instruct the synthesis agent to always prefer the most recent figure and ignore older ones
Have each subagent settle disagreements with the other subagents before returning its findings
Tell the synthesis agent never to describe any difference between sources as a contradiction
why: Without dates, a change over time looks like a conflict. With a date on every finding, the synthesis agent can present the figures as a trend, 12% in 2021 and 31% in 2025. Always preferring the newest figure hides that trend, subagents work in isolation and cannot see each other's findings, and banning the word contradiction would also hide real conflicts.

q: To fit a downstream budget, an intermediate agent condenses 60 findings into 15 bullets. Three of the findings made the same claim, each from a different report. Which representation of the merged claim best preserves provenance?
opts: The claim once, with a note that three sources agree
The claim once, with the source of only the first finding, to keep the bullet short
The claim once, with no sources, because corroboration makes citations unnecessary
The claim once, with all three source URLs and a supporting excerpt from each
why: Claim-source mappings must be preserved and merged when findings are combined: the merged record keeps every source and its excerpt, so each can be audited and the corroboration is visible. A bare count cannot be traced, one source throws away the other two, and dropping sources removes the very thing that makes a claim checkable.

q: A final report covers 20 findings. Twelve are supported by several agreeing sources, and eight involve sources that disagree on method or numbers. How should the report be structured?
opts: Rank all 20 findings in one list by publication date, newest first, so that readers see recent work at the top
Include only the twelve established findings so that the report speaks with one clear and confident voice
Present all 20 in a single list and add hedging words such as "some say" to each of the disputed ones
Separate established from contested findings, keeping each source's own characterization and methods
why: Separating established from contested findings shows readers where confidence is high and where it is not, and keeping the sources' own wording and methods lets them weigh the disagreement. A date-ordered list mixes the two, omitting the contested eight conceals the uncertainty, and hedging words do not say who disagrees or why.

q: A synthesis agent converts everything it finds into bullet points. Quarterly revenue figures for four companies become hard to compare, and a news story loses its narrative thread. What is the best fix?
opts: Render each type in its natural form: financial data as tables, news as prose, technical findings as structured lists
Present all content as tables, because tables are the most precise way to show any kind of information to a reader
Present all content as continuous prose, so that the whole report reads as a single coherent narrative from start to end
Output everything as JSON and leave the decision about how to display it to a downstream formatter at a later stage
why: Different kinds of content carry their information differently, so forcing one uniform format destroys some of it. Tables suit comparisons of numbers, prose suits narrative, and structured lists suit technical points. A single table format flattens stories, prose buries numbers, and passing the decision to a hypothetical formatter leaves the problem unsolved.

q: A document-analysis subagent finds two different values for the same metric in two reports. Which two actions fit the recommended pattern? (Choose two.)
opts: Include both values in its structured output, each annotated with its source and date
Keep only the value from the report with more pages, since it is probably more thorough
Let the coordinator decide how to reconcile the values before the findings go to synthesis
Average the two values and report the result as the finding
Leave the metric out entirely, since the reports disagree
why: The analysis agent reports the conflict openly, with both values annotated; the coordinator, which sees the whole task, decides how to reconcile it before synthesis. Picking by page count, averaging and omitting the metric each resolve the disagreement silently, on weak grounds, or by throwing the evidence away.

q: When two credible sources give different figures for the same statistic, the synthesis step should choose one value so that the report reads cleanly.
opts: True
False
why: Silently choosing hides a real disagreement. The report should keep both values, annotate each with its source (and method or date where known), and let the reader or coordinator reconcile them.

q: Requiring publication or data-collection dates in subagents' structured outputs helps the synthesis step tell a real conflict from a change over time.
opts: True
False
why: A statistic that moved between 2021 and 2025 describes a trend, not a contradiction. Dates on every finding let the synthesis step interpret differences correctly.
